prompt: Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 in which of the following ways?

choices.text: The type of soil was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The type of soil was kept the same in both experiments; only the volume of water sprinkled changed.

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the mass of soil eroded
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the mass of soil eroded.

choices.text: The volume of water sprinkled was 2 L of water in Experiment 1 and 4 L of water in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: The slope angle of the tray was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of slope angle.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 using 4 L of water; everything else, including the values of slope angle and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can using 2 L of water. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using 4 L of water, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: Increasing launch angle increases range.
choices.rationale: The results rise only over the first part of the range, then fall.

choices.text: The compression of the spring determines range.
choices.rationale: The compression of the spring was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

choices.text: Increasing launch angle decreases range.
choices.rationale: The results fall only over the last part of the range, after rising.

choices.text: Range is greatest at an intermediate launch angle and lower at both higher and lower values.
choices.rationale: Correct. The measured value rises to a maximum partway through the range and then falls.

explanation: Reading the results in order of launch angle, the horizontal distance the ball traveled increased, then decreased, which supports: "Range is greatest at an intermediate launch angle and lower at both higher and lower values."

stimulus.title: Launch Angle and Range
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students used a spring launcher to fire the same ball at a set angle above the horizontal, always with the spring compressed by the same amount. They measured the horizontal distance from the launcher to the landing point. Each angle was fired three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the horizontal distance the ball traveled): at 20°, 20.6 m; at 30°, 26.3 m; at 40°, 28.4 m; at 50°, 27.2 m; at 60°, 23.0 m; at 70°, 16.6 m.

prompt: In Experiment 1, the experimenters repeated each measurement several times and recorded the average. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Increase the range of speed that could be tested
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement does not change which values of speed are tested.

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the car and its tires the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

choices.text: Make the stopping distance change more in response to speed
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement cannot change the size of the real effect.

explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Speed and Stopping Distance
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
On a closed test track, a driver brought the same car to each test speed, then braked as hard as possible when a signal light flashed. The distance from the signal to the stopping point was measured. Each speed was tested three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the stopping distance): at 40 km/h, 17.5 m; at 60 km/h, 32.6 m; at 80 km/h, 51.8 m; at 100 km/h, 75.3 m; at 120 km/h, 103.0 m.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters had run one more trial in Experiment 1 at a time of 27.5 min. Based on the results, the temperature of the water in that trial would most likely have been:

choices.text: between 32.4 °C and 36.5 °C
choices.rationale: Correct. 27.5 min is between the tested values 25 min and 30 min, whose results were 32.4 and 36.5.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 29.3 °C
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 29.3 °C and 32.4 °C
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to time between 30 min and 35 min.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 49.6 °C
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

explanation: The results change steadily with time, so a trial at 27.5 min should give a value between those of its neighbors, 32.4 and 36.5 °C.

stimulus.title: Cooling Curve
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students poured hot water into a cup and recorded the water's temperature with a digital thermometer every five minutes. The cup sat on a table in a room at a constant temperature.
Results (the temperature of the water): at 15 min, 49.6 °C; at 20 min, 42.1 °C; at 25 min, 36.5 °C; at 30 min, 32.4 °C; at 35 min, 29.3 °C.

prompt: The experimenters tested 5 different values of the depth below the surface rather than just two. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Make each individual measurement of the water temperature more precise than it would otherwise be
choices.rationale: The precision of a single measurement depends on the instrument and repetition, not on how many values of the independent variable are tested.

choices.text: Show how the water temperature changes across the whole range, not just at its two ends
choices.rationale: Correct. Two points can only show a difference; several points show the shape of the relationship.

choices.text: Remove the need to hold the location of the boat constant during the trials
choices.rationale: Testing more values does not replace controlling other variables.

choices.text: Keep the water temperature the same from one trial to the next so that the trials could be compared
choices.rationale: The dependent variable is measured, not held constant; it is expected to change.

explanation: Measuring at several values of depth lets the experimenters see the pattern of the relationship, not just whether the two ends differ.

stimulus.title: Lake Temperature and Depth
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
From a boat anchored over the deepest part of a lake, students lowered a thermometer probe on a marked cable and recorded the water temperature at several depths. All readings were taken within one hour at midday.
Results (the water temperature): at 4 m, 13.6 °C; at 6 m, 11.1 °C; at 8 m, 9.5 °C; at 10 m, 8.6 °C; at 12 m, 8.0 °C.

prompt: Which of the following changes to Experiment 1 would most improve the reliability of its results?

choices.text: Record the stopping distance to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each speed and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Test fewer values of speed so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

choices.text: Allow the car and its tires to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

prompt: Which of the following best describes how the procedure of Experiment 2 differed from that of Experiment 1?

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the stretch of the spring
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the stretch of the spring.

choices.text: The mass hung from the spring was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of mass.

choices.text: The spring used was Spring A in Experiment 1 and Spring B in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: The way the length was measured was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The way the length was measured was kept the same in both experiments; only the spring used changed.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 using Spring B, made of thicker wire; everything else, including the values of mass and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students hung a spring from a stand using Spring A, made of thin wire and measured its unstretched length. They hung a mass from the spring, waited for it to stop moving, and measured the new length. The stretch is the difference between the two lengths. Masses were added in steps. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using Spring B, made of thicker wire, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Based on Experiment 1, which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The starting temperature of the water determines water temperature.
choices.rationale: The starting temperature of the water was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

choices.text: Water temperature is greatest at an intermediate time and lower at both higher and lower values.
choices.rationale: The results never reverse direction, so there is no intermediate maximum.

choices.text: Time has no effect on water temperature.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

choices.text: Increasing time decreases water temperature.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a smaller measured value.

explanation: Reading the results in order of time, the temperature of the water decreased, which supports: "Increasing time decreases water temperature."

stimulus.title: Antibiotic Dose and Bacterial Growth
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students spread 0.1 mL of a bacterial culture onto agar plates containing a known concentration of an antibiotic. After 24 hours they counted the colonies on each plate. Three plates were prepared for each concentration and the average count was recorded.
Results (the number of colonies): at 5 µg/mL, 194 colonies; at 10 µg/mL, 100 colonies; at 15 µg/mL, 51 colonies; at 20 µg/mL, 26 colonies; at 25 µg/mL, 14 colonies.

prompt: If Experiment 1 were extended with a trial at 0.15 A, the voltage across the resistor would most likely have been:

choices.text: between 6.7 V and 10.0 V
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to current between 0.2 A and 0.3 A.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 3.3 V
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 3.3 V and 6.7 V
choices.rationale: Correct. 0.15 A is between the tested values 0.1 A and 0.2 A, whose results were 3.3 and 6.7.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 20.1 V
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

explanation: The results change steadily with current, so a trial at 0.15 A should give a value between those of its neighbors, 3.3 and 6.7 V.

stimulus.title: Current and Voltage
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students connected a resistor to a variable power supply and an ammeter. They adjusted the supply to set the current to each test value and read the voltage across the resistor with a voltmeter.
Results (the voltage across the resistor): at 0.1 A, 3.3 V; at 0.2 A, 6.7 V; at 0.3 A, 10.0 V; at 0.4 A, 13.4 V; at 0.5 A, 16.7 V; at 0.6 A, 20.1 V.

stimulus.title: Spring Stretch
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students hung a spring from a stand and measured its unstretched length. They hung a mass from the spring, waited for it to stop moving, and measured the new length. The stretch is the difference between the two lengths. Masses were added in steps.
Results (the stretch of the spring): at 100 g, 5.7 cm; at 150 g, 8.5 cm; at 200 g, 11.3 cm; at 250 g, 14.2 cm; at 300 g, 17.0 cm.
